title: "Was/now" prices and the anchor trick
description: A crossed-out high price makes the current price feel small. That feeling is manufactured — the crossed-out number is an anchor, not a fact about value.

body.heading: How anchoring works
paragraphs: Show someone a jacket marked "was $200, now $80" and $80 feels like a steal. Show the same jacket at $80 with no history and it feels like a decision. The first number you see drags your judgement toward it; psychologists call this anchoring, and price tags are built on it.

The anchor only works if the "was" price was real — an actual price at which the item genuinely sold, for a reasonable time. In many places, rules require exactly that, yet some "was" prices are brief, rare, or from a different, dearer version of the product.

body.heading: Questions that cut the anchor
paragraphs: Ignore the crossed-out number and judge the current price on its own: what would this be worth to me, and what do similar items cost elsewhere? A two-minute comparison search usually reveals whether "now" is special or simply normal.

Sale seasons deserve the same calm. Some shops raise prices shortly before a sale so the discount looks dramatic. Price-tracking websites and your own memory of last month's price are better guides than the banner.

body.heading: A discount is not income
paragraphs: "I saved $120" is only true if you would genuinely have paid the $200. Spending $80 you never planned to spend is not saving $120; it is spending $80. The anchor's favourite trick is making expenditure feel like earnings.

None of this means never enjoying a genuine sale. It means letting your own valuation lead: decide what the item is worth to you first, then check the price. When the price is below your valuation, buy happily — the anchor never gets a vote.

takeaway: Judge every offer by the "now" price against the wider market, and remember: money not spent is the only discount that is always real.
